title: Outreach pricing and reviews (2026)
summary: What Outreach (outreach.ai) actually costs in 2026, its gated Amplify tiers and AI-credit model, honest reviewer themes, and who it fits.
body_markdown:
Outreach (now outreach.ai) does not publish prices. Its Amplify plans (Core, Plus, and Pro) combine a per-seat license with AI-credit consumption, and every quote runs through sales on an annual contract. Third-party buyers report roughly $100 to $165/user/month. Reviewers rate its sequencing engine highly and its setup work less so.


## Outreach pricing at a glance (2026)


Plan


What it covers


Pricing


Amplify Core


Core sequencing, dialer, deal and pipeline workflows, reporting

Amplify Pro


Full platform, Omni agent, advanced governance and admin controls


Custom, contact sales (per seat + AI credits)


All figures are gated. The best-sourced estimate from third-party buyers is roughly $100 to $165/user/month, and this is an estimate, not a published rate. Contracts are annual, and AI-credit consumption is metered on top of the seat license.


## How much does Outreach cost in practice?


Plan on more than the per-seat sticker. Outreach sells annual contracts with seat minimums, and the newer AI-credit model means the parts most teams actually want (agent actions, the Omni agent, richer automation) draw down a credit balance that sits on top of the license. A team that under-provisions credits either throttles the AI or negotiates a mid-term increase.


Then there is the work around the tool. Outreach is a platform, not a plug-in, so most buyers budget for onboarding, admin time, and often a dedicated operations owner to build and maintain sequences, rulesets, and reporting. Reviewers report that the value is real once the system is dialed in, and that reaching that point takes weeks and a capable admin. For a 25-seat team at the middle of the reported range, the license alone lands in the low six figures a year, and credits, implementation, and admin headcount push the fully loaded number higher.


## What do the Amplify tiers include?


The Amplify tiers step up along two axes: how much of the AI workflow you unlock, and how much governance and admin control you have. Core covers the classic sales-engagement job, sequences, a dialer, deal and pipeline management, and reporting. Plus layers in deeper AI actions and forecasting. Pro opens the full platform, including the Omni agent and the advanced admin and governance controls that larger revenue teams need for approvals, permissions, and audit.


The important shift in 2026 is the move to consumption. Outreach positions itself as an AI revenue workflow platform, and the agent features are priced through AI credits instead of bundled flat into the seat. This is honest about how AI cost works, and it also means the quote you sign is not the cost you carry if usage climbs. For workflow specifics, see[outreach automation](https://www.artisan.co/blog/outreach-automation) .


## What are the hidden costs of Outreach?


The line items that surprise buyers are annual lock-in, seat minimums, AI-credit overages, and implementation. Because pricing is negotiated, two similar companies can pay materially different rates for the same configuration, which makes budgeting harder and puts a premium on buyer bargaining power.


Credits are the newest variable. As teams lean on agent features, credit consumption becomes a live cost that finance has to forecast, not a fixed subscription. Add professional services for onboarding and the internal admin time to run the platform, and the effective cost per productive rep sits well above the headline per-seat figure. None of this makes Outreach a bad buy. It does mean the real number is the loaded one.


## What do reviewers say about Outreach?


The consensus is that Outreach is a mature, deep sales-engagement platform that rewards teams with the operational muscle to run it. Reviewers report that its sequencing engine, deal and pipeline workflows, reporting, and integrations are best in class, and that governance and admin controls hold up for large, structured sales orgs. Its deliverability and sending controls receive consistent credit.


The complaints cluster around cost and complexity. Reviewers report that pricing is opaque and negotiated, that seat-based economics add up fast as teams grow, and that the platform is heavy to configure and administer, with a learning curve that can slow smaller teams. Some note that its AI features, while improving quickly, are newer than its core sequencer and still maturing. The through-line is that Outreach is powerful, but you pay for it in dollars and in operational overhead. For the broader category, see[the best sales engagement platforms](https://www.artisan.co/blog/the-best-sales-engagement-platforms) .


## Who is Outreach best for, and not for?


Outreach best fits large, structured revenue teams that already run a disciplined sales motion and want an enterprise-grade engagement layer with strong governance, reporting, and integrations, plus the admin resources to own it. If you have a RevOps (revenue operations) function and a lot of reps that execute sequences, it is a category standard for a reason.


It fits less well for small teams, or for buyers who want an AI that runs outbound instead of a system that helps reps run it. Outreach orchestrates people. Sequences, calls, replies, and follow-through still come from your reps. If the constraint you are solving for is headcount rather than rep efficiency, a per-seat orchestration platform makes the constraint more expensive, not less.


## Worth considering: Artisan


If you are evaluating Outreach because outbound is not producing enough pipeline, it is worth separating two different jobs. Outreach makes each rep more efficient at running a motion. Artisan runs the motion. Ava, Artisan's AI business development representative (BDR), owns the outbound job end to end: she finds best-fit leads from a database of over 250 million B2B professionals across over 200 countries, plus Artisan Local Data's over 250 million local businesses, enriches and prioritizes them with waterfall email and phone enrichment, launches personalized multichannel campaigns across email, social media, and the dialer, tests dozens of message variations, handles replies and objections from a knowledge base, and books meetings on the right rep's calendar with CRM-owner routing.


The autonomy is a dial, not a switch. You can keep Ava in review-and-approve mode, let her handle objections only, or run her fully autonomous, with plain-language escalation rules and a full audit trail. Larger teams often deploy her centrally from sales ops for AEs who never log in. It is the consolidation story too: one platform in place of the five to eight tools a lot of teams stitch together around a sequencer.


Pricing is the other contrast. Artisan is usage-based. You pay for work performed, not per seat, and there is a free trial, so cost tracks output instead of headcount. See[Artisan pricing](https://www.artisan.co/pricing) for the model. SaaStr's Chief AI Officer, Amelia Lerutte, said Artisan is now neck-and-neck with email, historically their top driver, in both output and closed-won revenue. For most teams that are weighing Outreach, the useful question is whether you need a better cockpit for your reps or an AI that does the flying. For a direct comparison, see[Artisan vs. Outreach](https://www.artisan.co/blog/artisan-vs-outreach) .


## FAQ


### How much does Outreach cost per user?


Outreach does not publish per-user pricing. Its Amplify plans combine a per-seat license with AI-credit consumption, and quotes are negotiated per deal on annual contracts. Third-party buyers report an effective range of roughly $100 to $165/user/month, before AI-credit usage, implementation, and admin overhead. Treat any specific figure as an estimate until you have a quote in hand.


### Is Outreach expensive?


For small teams, yes, relative to lighter sales-engagement tools. Outreach is priced as an enterprise platform with seat minimums, annual terms, and metered AI credits, and the fully loaded cost includes implementation and admin time. Larger revenue orgs with the operational muscle to run it tend to find the value justifies the price. Smaller teams often find the overhead outweighs the benefit.


### What is the Outreach Omni agent?


Omni is Outreach's AI agent, launched April 27, 2026, as part of its repositioning as an AI revenue workflow platform. It automates workflow actions across the engagement motion. Agent features like Omni are priced through AI-credit consumption on top of the per-seat license, so heavier agent usage increases cost. It is available on the higher Amplify tiers.


### Does Outreach have a free trial or free plan?


No. Outreach does not offer a public free plan or self-serve free trial. Access starts with a sales conversation and a demo, and pricing is quoted per deal on an annual contract. Buyers who want to try software before committing to an annual term should factor this into the evaluation timeline.


### What are cheaper alternatives to Outreach?


Salesloft is the closest peer, though it is also gated. For published per-seat pricing, look at Klenty (from around $50/user/month annually) and Reply.io (sequences from around $49 to $59 per user). These are lighter than Outreach. If the goal is fewer tools and an AI that runs outbound rather than another seat-based sequencer, Artisan uses a usage-based model. For more options, see[the best Outreach alternatives](https://www.artisan.co/blog/the-best-outreach-alternatives) ,[outreach io alternatives](https://www.artisan.co/blog/outreach-io-alternatives) , and[outreach tools](https://www.artisan.co/blog/outreach-tools) .


### Does Outreach replace SDRs?


No. Outreach is a sales-engagement platform that helps sales development reps (SDRs) run sequences, calls, and deals more efficiently. Your team still writes, sends, calls, and replies. If you want the prospecting-to-booking job handled by an AI instead of merely made faster for humans, this is a different category. Artisan's Ava owns the BDR workflow end to end, with human review and escalation controls.
